title: 牛肉麵真好吃 Beef Noodles Are Really Delicious

paras.text: Topic: 飲食 Food and Drink
• Learning the names of common foods and describing their taste.
• Learning to express likes for and make simple comments about food.
• Learning to describe what somebody can/can’t do and how well one does it.
• Learning to ask for help.

lines.zh: 很多人都說臺灣有不少有名的小吃。
lines.py: Hěn duō rén dōu shuō Táiwān yǒu bù shǎo yǒumíng de xiǎochī.

lines.zh: 是啊！牛肉麵、小籠包、臭豆腐…都很好吃。
lines.py: Shì a. Niúròu miàn, xiǎolóngbāo, chòu dòufǔ... dōu hěn hǎochī.

lines.zh: 牛肉麵。牛肉好吃，湯也好喝。
lines.py: Niúròu miàn. Niúròu hǎochī, tāng yě hǎohē.
Zhème hǎochī, wǒ hěn xiǎng chī.

lines.zh: 我知道一家有名的牛肉麵店，我們一起去吃，怎麼樣？
lines.py: Wǒ zhīdào yì jiā yǒumíng de niúròu miàn diàn. Wǒmen yìqǐ qù chī, zěnmeyàng?

lines.zh: 我們明天去。一定要點大碗的。
lines.py: Wǒmen míngtiān qù. Yídìng yào diǎn dà wǎn de.

translation.en: Many people say Taiwan has quite a few well-known light repasts.
That’s right. Beef noodles, xiaolongbao, stinky tofu... are all tasty.
What do you like to eat most?
Beef noodles. The beef tastes good and the soup is nice.
That tasty. I would like to have some.
I know a place that is well-known for its beef noodles. Let’s go together and have some. What do you say?
Let’s go tomorrow. You really have to order a large bowl.

items.en: measure word for restaurants, shops, etc.
xiaolongbao, e.g., small meat and cabbage-filled steamed buns

lines.zh: 昨天晚上那家餐廳的菜很好吃，可是有一點辣。
lines.py: Zuótiān wǎnshàng nà jiā cāntīng de cài hěn hǎochī, kěshì yǒu yìdiǎn là.

lines.zh: 我也怕辣，所以我喜歡自己做飯。
lines.py: Wǒ yě pà là, suǒyǐ wǒ xǐhuān zìjǐ zuòfàn.

lines.zh: 我做得不好。妳會做飯嗎？
lines.py: Wǒ zuò de bù hǎo. Nǐ huì zuòfàn ma?

lines.zh: 會。我的甜點也做得不錯。
lines.py: Huì. Wǒ de tiándiǎn yě zuò de búcuò.

lines.zh: 我最喜歡吃甜點。妳可以教我嗎？
lines.py: Wǒ zuì xǐhuān chī tiándiǎn. Nǐ kěyǐ jiāo wǒ ma?

lines.zh: 好的，這個週末，你到我家來。
lines.py: Hǎode, zhè ge zhōumò, nǐ dào wǒ jiā lái.

translation.en: The food at the restaurant last night was good, but it was a bit spicy.
I can’t take spicy (food), either. That is why I prefer to cook for myself.
I don’t cook well. Can you cook?
Yes. I make good desserts, too.
I like eating desserts most. Could you teach me?
Sure. Come over to my place this weekend.

blocks.en: I. 有一點 yǒu yìdiǎn slightly

paras.text: Function: 有一點 + State Verb suggests a slightly negative evaluation.

items.py: Zhè wǎn niúròu miàn yǒu yìdiǎn là.
items.en: This bowl of beef noodle is a little spicy.

items.py: Nà zhī shǒujī yǒu yìdiǎn guì.
items.en: That cell phone is a little expensive.

items.py: Tā de fángzi yǒu yìdiǎn jiù.
items.en: His house is a little old.

paras.text: Structures: Since this expression suggests negative evaluation, there is no negative form for the pattern. If the Vs has a positive meaning, it can’t be used in this pattern. For example, one can say, 這張照片有一點舊。Zhè zhāng zhàopiàn yǒu yìdiǎn jiù. ‘This photo is a little old’. However, you cannot say *他妹妹有一點漂亮 Tā mèimei yǒu yìdiǎn piàoliàng. ‘His younger sister is a little beautiful’.

items.prompt: A：你覺得臭豆腐怎麼樣？　B：我覺得臭豆腐＿＿＿＿＿＿。
A：你覺得那家餐廳的菜怎麼樣？　B：那家餐廳的菜＿＿＿＿＿＿。
A：牛肉麵好吃嗎？　B：好吃，可是＿＿＿＿＿＿。
A：那個包子怎麼樣？　B：好吃，可是我覺得＿＿＿＿＿＿。
A：他的手機是新的嗎？　B：不是新的，＿＿＿＿＿＿。

paras.text: Function: The complement marker 得 de follows the verb and introduces the complement, which describes the result or state of the action suggested by the verb.

items.py: Tā xué Zhōngwén xué de búcuò.
items.en: He has learned Chinese quite well.

items.zh: 王伯母做越南菜做得很好。
items.py: Wáng Bómǔ zuò Yuènán cài zuò de hěn hǎo.
items.en: Auntie Wang cooks Vietnamese food very well.

items.py: Zhè zhǒng shǒujī mài de hěn hǎo.
items.en: This type of cell phone sells well.

paras.text: Structures: When a complement is added to a transitive verb, several structural consequences follow.
1. When its object directly follows the verb, the verb is repeated before 得 de and the complement.

items.py: Nǐ zuòfàn zuò de zhēn hǎochī.

items.zh: 我的老師教中文教得很好。
items.py: Wǒ de lǎoshī jiāo Zhōngwén jiāo de hěn hǎo.

paras.text: 2. When the object appears at the front of the sentence, the verb is not repeated.

items.py: Fàn, tā zuò de zhēn hǎochī.
Zhōngwén, nǐ shuō de hěn hǎo.

items.zh: 這種甜點，他做得很好吃。
items.py: Zhè zhǒng tiándiǎn, tā zuò de hěn hǎochī.
items.en: He makes this kind of dessert very tasty.

items.py: Zhè zhī shǒujī mài de hěn piányí.
items.en: This cell phone is sold cheaply.

paras.text: Negation: Negation occurs only within the complement.

items.py: Tā zuò tiándiǎn zuò de bù hǎo.
items.en: He does not make desserts well.

items.zh: 王先生打網球打得不好。
items.py: Wáng Xiānshēng dǎ wǎngqiú dǎ de bù hǎo.
items.en: Mr. Wang does not play the tennis well.

items.py: Tā de kāfēi mài de bù hǎo.
items.en: His coffee does not sell well.

items.zh: 越南菜，這家店做得不好吃。
items.py: Yuènán cài, zhè jiā diàn zuò de bù hǎochī.
items.en: This shop does not cook Vietnamese food well.

items.py: Tā dǎ lánqiú dǎ de hǎo ma?
Zhōngwén, tā shuō de hǎo bù hǎo?

items.prompt: 你弟弟踢足球踢得怎麼樣？　他踢得＿＿＿＿＿＿。
他姐姐做甜點，做得好吃不好吃？　做得＿＿＿＿＿＿。
日本菜，你妹妹做得好不好？　我妹妹做＿＿＿＿＿＿。
這種手機賣得怎麼樣？　賣得＿＿＿＿＿＿。
他打網球打得好嗎？　打＿＿＿＿＿＿。

paras.text: Function: 會 huì indicates that these skills are acquired through learning.

items.en: His older brother knows how to play soccer.

items.zh: 他們兄弟姐妹都會游泳。
items.py: Tāmen xiōngdì jiěmèi dōu huì yóuyǒng.
items.en: All of those siblings know how to swim.

paras.text: Structures: 會 huì is an auxiliary verb and can be negated.

items.py: Tā de māma bú huì zuòfàn.
Wǒ māma bú huì zuò tiándiǎn.
items.en: My mom does not know how to make desserts.

items.zh: 我的家人都不會打棒球。
items.py: Wǒ de jiārén dōu bú huì dǎ bàngqiú.
items.en: None of the members of my family knows how to play baseball.
Do you know how to make desserts?

items.py: Tā dìdi huì tī zúqiú ma?
items.en: Does his younger brother know how to play football?

items.py: Nǐ huì bú huì shuō Zhōngwén?
items.en: Do you know how to speak Chinese?

items.py: Nǐ de jiějie huì bú huì zuòfàn?
items.en: Does your elder sister know how to cook?

items.prompt: A：他會不會做牛肉麵？　B：＿＿＿，他弟弟也會做。
A：你哥哥會不會打網球？　B：＿＿＿，你可以教他嗎？
A：我們都會打棒球，你呢？　B：我＿＿＿，可是我很想學。
A：我會踢足球，你呢？　B：我＿＿＿，你可以教我嗎？
A：小籠包和包子，我都會做，你呢？　B：我也＿＿＿。

paras.text: Function: The preposition 到 dào indicates the destination of a movement.

items.py: Tā zhè ge zhōumò dào Táiwān lái.
items.en: He is coming to Taiwan this weekend.

items.zh: 老師明天到臺北來。我們要和他一起吃晚飯。
items.py: Lǎoshī míngtiān dào Táiběi lái. Wǒmen yào hàn tā yìqǐ chī wǎnfàn.
items.en: The teacher is coming to Taipei tomorrow. We are having dinner with him.

items.zh: 想吃牛肉麵嗎？明天我們可以到那家店去。
items.py: Xiǎng chī niúròu miàn ma? Míngtiān wǒmen kěyǐ dào nà jiā diàn qù.
items.en: Would you like to have beef noodles? We can go to that shop tomorrow.

items.zh: 我可以教你中文，明天到我家來吧！
items.py: Wǒ kěyǐ jiāo nǐ Zhōngwén, míngtiān dào wǒ jiā lái ba!
items.en: I can teach you Chinese. Go ahead and come to my house tomorrow.

paras.text: Structures:
Negation: Negation is always done by placing a negator in front of a preposition, not the main verb.

items.zh: 王先生明天不到臺北來。
items.py: Wáng Xiānshēng míngtiān bú dào Táiběi lái.
items.en: Mr. Wang is not coming to Taipei tomorrow.

items.zh: 那家的越南菜不好吃。他們不到那家餐廳去。
items.py: Nà jiā de Yuènán cài bù hǎochī. Tāmen bú dào nà jiā cāntīng qù.
items.en: That shop’s Vietnamese food doesn’t taste good. They don’t go to that restaurant.

items.zh: 他晚上去看電影，不到我家來，你呢？
items.py: Tā wǎnshàng qù kàn diànyǐng, bú dào wǒ jiā lái, nǐ ne?
items.en: He is going to go to a movie tonight and will not be coming to my house. How about you?

paras.text: Questions: 到 dào can be used to form A-not-A questions.

items.py: Nǐ mèimei dào bú dào Táiwān lái?
items.en: Is your younger sister coming to Taiwan?

items.py: Tāmen dào bú dào wǒ jiā lái?
items.en: Are they coming to my house?

paras.text: Usage: The destination marker 到 dào is a preposition and another verb serves as the main verb in the sentence (e.g., 來 lái ‘come’ or 去 qù ‘go’). In Taiwan and Southern China, however, 到 dào is often used as a verb, like 來 lái or 去 qù.

items.zh: 這麼多家餐廳，我們要到哪一家？
items.py: Zhème duō jiā cāntīng, wǒmen yào dào nǎ yì jiā?
items.en: There are so many restaurants. Which one should we go?

items.zh: 他們明天晚上要到王老師家。你想去嗎？
items.py: Tāmen míngtiān wǎnshàng yào dào Wáng lǎoshī jiā. Nǐ xiǎng qù ma?
items.en: They are going to Teacher Wang’s house tomorrow evening. Would you like to go?

paras.text: Goal: Learning to describe what someone can/can’t do and how well s/he does it.

Task: There is going to be a talent contest at school. Find out what your classmates can do and how well they can do it. Record your findings. Ask questions using phrases that you learned, like 做甜點、游泳、照相、打籃球、踢足球、做小籠包、打網球. (Make desserts, swim, take pictures, play basketball, play soccer, make xiaolongbao, play tennis.)

paras.text: Goal: Learning to ask for help.

Task: From the survey you completed in Task III, find one item that interests you and ask the person if s/he could teach you how do to it, e.g., 我想學做小籠包，你可以教我嗎？(I want to learn how to make xiaolongbao. Can you teach me?)

Lines in front of roadside food stands are a familiar scene in Taiwan. Food stalls usually open for business at fixed times and in fixed locations. As long as the food sold at a stall is fresh, inexpensive, and good, you can be sure there will be a long queue in front of it regardless of the weather.
With a little pocket change, you can buy delicious baozi, scallion pancakes, wheel-barrel cakes, or pan-fried dumplings. It is little wonder that there are queues on almost every street corner.

Street vendors are very common in Taiwan. They are the product of farmer’s markets and temple festivals of an agricultural society of a time passed. Today, street vendors are seen in scenic sites, residential areas, outskirts of markets, business district surroundings, on arcaded corridors, on the streets, outside examination sites, and during temple festivals. The selections of vendors range from daily goods to food to souvenirs. Since street vendors are very mobile, they sometimes affect traffic, disturb quiet neighborhoods, or scar cityscape. If street vendors could be regulated, they could add to the excitement and beauty of the city.

paras.text: Pinyin Rules
As with “zh-/zhi,” “ch-/chi,” and “sh-/shi,” when “z-,” “c-,” and “s-” stand alone, “i” is added to form zi, ci, and si.
When “u” is followed by other vowels, but is not preceded by a consonant, change the “u” to “w,” as in “u” + “ei” → wéi 微 in Lesson Four and “u” + “o” → wǒ 我 in Lesson 1.

When the vowel “i” is followed by “ou” but is not preceded by a consonant, change the “i” to “y” to form 有 yǒu (Refer to Lesson 2). When a consonant precedes the “i” + “ou” compound, the “o” is omitted and it becomes “-iu,” e.g., 牛 → niú, 六 → liù. The “o,” however, is still pronounced, e.g., → “ni(o)ú” and “li(o)ù.”

blocks.en: Introduction to Chinese Characters — The Earliest Chinese Characters

paras.text: There are three general beliefs regarding the origin of Chinese characters:
1. Chinese characters were created by a person by the name of Cangjie.
2. Chinese characters originated from the eight trigrams and rope-knotting.
3. Chinese characters originated from pictograms. This is also the most widely adopted belief among scholars.

Characters were not created by any single person, at any single time, or at any specific place. They were developed and accumulated over time. Most scholars believe that Chinese characters originated from pictures or drawings and slowly became signs and characters.

The Chinese characters we see and use today have undergone many thousands of years of evolution, from the oracle bone script of the Shang Dynasty to bronze script and Large Seal script of the Zhou Dynasty to the Small Seal script that was adopted after the Qin Dynasty and used to unite the Six Kingdoms. These scripts are classified as ancient scripts. During the Han Dynasty, the symmetrical and rounded look of Small Seal script was modified to become more rectangular and orderly, making writing easier and faster. This came to known as Clerical script. The Regular script we use now evolved directly from the Clerical script. In other words, the standardized characters in use today were shaped and formed during the Han Dynasty.
